articles.title: First fMRI study of mescaline reveals altered sensory filtering and brain networks
articles.summary: A groundbreaking brain imaging study in awake rats reveals that the psychedelic mescaline uniquely alters brain function. The drug reduces cerebellum activity while boosting global connectivity, shifting how the brain processes rewards and filters sensory information.

articles.summary: arXiv:2609.25134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a probabilistic perspective on large language models (LLMs), developed with the aim of bringing together, in a single self-contained account, tools that are usually treated separately across the literature. LLMs are described through probability measures on the set of sequences of tokens, specified via their autoregressive conditional distributions. articles.title: A theory of plasticity: capacity for change as inverse configurational constraint
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.25312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plasticity is invoked across the sciences to explain how systems can change, yet it is inferred from the very change it is meant to explain. A system may have many alternatives, realize none and still be plastic. Another may be driven far toward its only alternative, but the magnitude of that change does not establish its plasticity. What matters for plasticity is not how far the system moves but how strongly its present configuration constrains alternatives. articles.title: Deep Learning in Infant Functional Neuroimaging: Challenges, Advances, and Future Directions
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.26688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Infancy is a critical developmental window characterized by rapid functional brain reorganization, during which large-scale networks emerge, individualized connectome signatures continue to form, and early deviations may shape long-term cognitive and clinical outcomes. articles.title: Fear of the unknown is linked to lower life satisfaction and heightened death anxiety
articles.summary: People who struggle with uncertainty tend to report lower life satisfaction. According to new research, this link is deeply existential, intertwining a fear of the unknown with a lower sense of purpose and higher death anxiety.

articles.title: Standard brain scans might misread oxygen metabolism in large portions of the cortex
articles.summary: A recent brain imaging study reveals that standard fMRI scans can yield backward metabolic readings in nearly half of responding brain regions, challenging conventional interpretations of how neural activity is mapped.

articles.title: Orexin neurons act as an effort-tracking system in the brain
articles.summary: A new study reveals that specialized brain cells called orexin neurons act as an effort-tracking system. By firing when a reward is expected, these cells help the brain decide if a goal is actually worth the physical effort.

articles.title: Social anxiety drives people to conform specifically to negative feedback
articles.summary: People with high social anxiety tend to change their own emotions to match negative peer feedback, while mostly ignoring positive feedback. Brain wave data reveals this biased conformity is driven by intense, prolonged mental effort.

articles.title: Stem cells reverse stroke damage and restore movement in mice
articles.summary: Stem cell transplants helped regenerate stroke-damaged brain tissue in mice, producing new neurons and restoring lost motor function. The treatment also improved blood vessels, inflammation, and the blood-brain barrier, raising hopes that a similar approach could eventually help repair the human brain after stroke.

articles.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
articles.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a possible cause of long COVID fatigue and brain fog
articles.summary: Researchers have found evidence that long COVID may damage dopamine releasing neurons in the brain, potentially explaining persistent fatigue, low motivation, slowed movement, and memory difficulties. The discovery could lead to new treatments that target the brain's dopamine system.

articles.title: Consciousness may have evolved to solve a problem that pure intelligence couldn’t handle, fascinating new theory suggests
articles.summary: We often assume a smart enough AI will eventually become conscious. But a new theoretical framework argues consciousness evolved specifically for biological self-preservation—meaning today's highly capable AI lacks the survival stakes to ever truly "wake up."

articles.title: Scientists discover previously unknown “mitochondrial plaques” in Alzheimer’s disease brains
articles.summary: When the brain's cellular recycling system breaks down in Alzheimer's disease, damaged mitochondria pile up inside nerve fibers. Researchers have now identified these clusters as "mitochondrial plaques," revealing a new pathological feature that could unlock novel treatments.

articles.title: Antagonistic narcissism is linked to cold feelings toward psychologists
articles.summary: People with antagonistic narcissistic traits often view mental health treatment negatively because they harbor cold feelings toward psychologists and psychiatrists. However, a recent study reveals that self-promotional narcissistic traits might actually encourage more favorable views of therapy.
